ns2:section.sectionText: Indigenous peoples have long and rich traditions of governance and political philosophies that have shaped institutions and informed diplomacies amongst each other and with European nations. This course examines those histories, looking particularly at the resurgence of indigenous governance, sovereignty, and resistance in recent years. What is at stake for indigenous peoples and governments? What conditions and values are necessary for decolonial leadership and action? How do native nations resist discourses of dependency and move toward self-determination and self-sufficiency? What might indigenous control of colonialist economies such as gaming and tourism entail? What role does language revitalization play in the decolonization of indigenous nations? Students will examine these questions and trace them through histories of indigenous governance in North America, Hawai'i, and New Zealand/Aotearoa.
